statement: Let $f\colon [0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be [measurable](c:measurable-function) and bounded on every bounded interval, with $f(t)\to L$ as $t\to\infty$. Then the [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) $F(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ exists for $s>0$, and $sF(s)\to L$ as $s\to 0^+$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) and bounded on $[0,T]$ for every $T>0$.
The [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $L=\lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)$ exists and is a real number.

conclusion: The integral $F(s)$ converges for every $s>0$, and $\lim_{s\to 0^+} sF(s)=L$.

proofs.name: Substitution and dominated convergence
proofs.slogan: Rescale the integral to the fixed weight $e^{-u}$, then pass to the limit under the integral sign.
proofs.scope: The Abelian direction: a limit of $f$ gives a limit of $sF(s)$, for real-valued $f$. The converse direction and the control form with poles of $F$ need further hypotheses and are not proved here.

roles.why: Local boundedness and measurability make the integrals defined and, with the limit, give one global bound.
The limit makes $f(u/s)$ tend to $L$ for each fixed $u>0$, and bounds $f$ near infinity.

steps.slogan: Bound $f$ on the whole half-line by one constant $M$.
steps.detail: Choose $T$ with $|f(t)|\le |L|+1$ for $t\ge T$. On $[0,T]$ the function is bounded by hypothesis, so $|f|\le M$ on $[0,\infty)$. Hence $\int_0^\infty e^{-st}|f(t)|\,dt\le M/s$, and $F(s)$ exists for $s>0$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $u=st$ to move $s$ into the argument of $f$.
steps.detail: For $s>0$ the substitution gives $sF(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}f(u/s)\,du$. The weight $e^{-u}$ no longer depends on $s$ and has integral $1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the integrand tends to $e^{-u}L$ for each fixed $u>0$.
steps.detail: If $s\to 0^+$, then $u/s\to\infty$, so $f(u/s)\to L$ by the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) hypothesis. Hence $e^{-u}f(u/s)\to e^{-u}L$.

steps.slogan: Dominate every integrand by the integrable function $Me^{-u}$.
steps.detail: By step 1, $|e^{-u}f(u/s)|\le Me^{-u}$ for all $s>0$ and $u\ge 0$. Also $\int_0^\infty Me^{-u}\,du=M<\infty$.

steps.slogan: Exchange the limit and the integral to get $sF(s)\to L$.
steps.detail: Take any sequence $s_n\to 0^+$. Dominated convergence gives $\lim sF(s_n)=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}L\,du=L$. The sequence was arbitrary, so $sF(s)\to L$ as $s\to 0^+$.

concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurability makes the Laplace integral well defined.
concepts.c:laplace-transform: The transform $F$ is the object whose scaled limit is computed.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-function: The limit of $f$ gives the bound and the pointwise limit.

source.note: The classical Abelian argument for the Laplace transform (substitution and dominated convergence), written out here.

statement: Let $f$ on the unit circle be $e^{V}$, with $V$ smooth, times Fisher-Hartwig factors at distinct points $z_0,\dots,z_m$: a root singularity $|z-z_j|^{2\alpha_j}$ with $\operatorname{Re}\alpha_j>-1/2$ and a jump of size $\beta_j$, where $\beta_j-\beta_k\notin\mathbb{Z}$ and $|\operatorname{Re}(\beta_j-\beta_k)|<1$. Then the [Toeplitz determinant](c:toeplitz-determinant) satisfies $D_n(f)=\exp\big(nV_0+\sum_{k\ge1}kV_kV_{-k}\big)\prod_j n^{\alpha_j^2-\beta_j^2}\,E\,(1+o(1))$, with $E$ an explicit constant.

hypotheses.text: The symbol is $e^{V}$ times Fisher-Hartwig factors at distinct points $z_0,\dots,z_m$ of the circle, and $V$ is smooth with Fourier coefficients $V_k$.
Every root-singularity strength has $\operatorname{Re}\alpha_j>-1/2$.
The jump parameters satisfy $\beta_j-\beta_k\notin\mathbb{Z}$ for $j\ne k$ and $|\operatorname{Re}(\beta_j-\beta_k)|<1$.

conclusion: The $n\times n$ Toeplitz determinants $D_n(f)$ have the stated Fisher-Hartwig asymptotics as $n\to\infty$.

proofs.name: Riemann-Hilbert analysis
proofs.slogan: Express the Toeplitz determinant through a Riemann-Hilbert problem, solve it by steepest descent, and integrate a differential identity.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof of the Toeplitz case; the parametrices and the uniform error bounds rest on the cited paper. The Hankel and Toeplitz+Hankel determinants of the same paper are other members of the family and are not covered.

roles.why: The smooth part gives the global parametrix and the known starting asymptotics.
The bound $\operatorname{Re}\alpha_j>-1/2$ keeps the weight integrable and the local parametrices defined.
Non-integer differences of the jumps keep the local parametrices distinct and the error uniform.

steps.slogan: Relate $D_n(f)$ to orthogonal polynomials and a [Riemann-Hilbert problem](c:riemann-hilbert-problem).
steps.detail: The ratio $D_{n+1}(f)/D_n(f)$ is the squared norm of the $n$-th monic orthogonal polynomial for the weight $f$ on the circle. These polynomials solve a $2\times2$ Riemann-Hilbert problem whose jump holds $f$ and $z^{-n}$. The singularities of $f$ make the jump singular at the points $z_j$.

steps.slogan: Derive differential identities for $\log D_n$ along a path of symbols.
steps.detail: Vary $V$, $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_j$ along a path of symbols $f_t$. The derivative of $\log D_n(f_t)$ is written through the solution of the Riemann-Hilbert problem, so the task becomes the asymptotics of that solution.

steps.slogan: Solve the Riemann-Hilbert problem asymptotically by Deift-Zhou steepest descent.
steps.detail: Open lenses on the circle, build a global parametrix from the Szego function of the smooth part and the singular factors, and glue local parametrices at each $z_j$. Bessel functions model a pure root singularity, and confluent hypergeometric functions model a jump with a root singularity.

steps.slogan: Bound the errors uniformly in the parameters and read off the differential identity.
steps.detail: A small-norm argument shows that the exact solution differs from the parametrices by a small error, uniform on compact parameter sets. The differential identities then give the derivative of $\log D_n(f_t)$ as an explicit leading term plus a uniformly small error.

steps.slogan: Integrate along the path from a symbol with known asymptotics to $f$.
steps.detail: Start from the smooth symbol $e^{V}$ with $\alpha_j=\beta_j=0$, where the strong Szego theorem gives $\log D_n=nV_0+\sum kV_kV_{-k}+o(1)$. Integrating the explicit leading terms in $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_j$ produces the factors $n^{\alpha_j^2-\beta_j^2}$ and the constant $E$ built from Barnes $G$-values.

concepts.c:toeplitz-determinant: The determinant $D_n(f)$ is the quantity whose asymptotics is computed.
concepts.c:riemann-hilbert-problem: The problem encodes the orthogonal polynomials and yields the differential identity.

source.ref: P. Deift, A. Its and I. Krasovsky, Asymptotics of Toeplitz, Hankel, and Toeplitz+Hankel determinants with Fisher-Hartwig singularities, Annals of Mathematics 174 (2011), 1243-1299
source.note: The paper proves the generalized conjecture of Fisher-Hartwig, Basor and Tracy in the nondegenerate case; the steps follow its Riemann-Hilbert proof.

statement: Every finite-dimensional [associative](c:associative-algebra) real [division algebra](c:division-algebra) is isomorphic, as an algebra over $\mathbb{R}$, to $\mathbb{R}$, to $\mathbb{C}$ or to the [quaternions](c:quaternion) $\mathbb{H}$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is a [finite-dimensional](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) real vector space.
The product of $A$ is bilinear and associative, with an identity $1\ne 0$.
Every nonzero element of $A$ has a two-sided inverse.

conclusion: The algebra $A$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{H}$ as a real algebra.

proofs.name: Commutant of a copy of the complex numbers
proofs.slogan: Find a copy of $\mathbb{C}$ in $A$, split $A$ by commuting and anticommuting elements, and read off the quaternion relations.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $A=\mathbb{R}$ there is nothing to prove, and if the anticommuting part is zero the proof gives $A=\mathbb{C}$.

roles.why: Finite dimension makes each element algebraic and bounds the dimensions of the two parts.
Associativity makes $\mathbb{R}[x]$ a commutative ring and conjugation by $i$ an automorphism.
Absence of zero divisors makes minimal polynomials irreducible and multiplication by $j$ injective.

steps.slogan: Find an element $i$ with $i^2=-1$ when $A\ne\mathbb{R}$.
steps.detail: Take $x\in A\setminus\mathbb{R}$. Its powers are dependent, so $x$ has a real [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) $p$, which is irreducible because $A$ has no zero divisors. Hence $\deg p\le 2$, and $\deg p=2$ because $x\notin\mathbb{R}$, so $\mathbb{R}[x]\cong\mathbb{C}$ contains such an $i$.

steps.slogan: Split $A$ into the elements that commute and anticommute with $i$.
steps.detail: The map $\sigma(a)=iai^{-1}$ satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$, because $i^2=-1$ is central. So $A=A_+\oplus A_-$ with $A_\pm=\{a: ia=\pm ai\}$, and $A_+$ is the commutant of $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}[i]$.

steps.slogan: Show that the commuting part $A_+$ equals $\mathbb{C}$.
steps.detail: For $a\in A_+$, the ring $\mathbb{C}[a]$ is a commutative finite-dimensional domain over $\mathbb{C}$, hence a field. A finite extension of the [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field) field $\mathbb{C}$ is $\mathbb{C}$, so $a\in\mathbb{C}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the anticommuting part $A_-$ is zero or two-dimensional.
steps.detail: Suppose $0\ne j\in A_-$. Left multiplication by $j$ is injective and maps $A_+$ into $A_-$ and $A_-$ into $A_+$. So $2=\dim A_+\le\dim A_-\le\dim A_+=2$, and $A_-=j\mathbb{C}$.

steps.slogan: Normalize $j$ so that $j^2=-1$.
steps.detail: Since $j^2$ commutes with $i$, $j^2=z\in\mathbb{C}$. As $j$ commutes with $j^2$ and $jz=\bar z j$, $z$ is real. If $z>0$, then $(j-\sqrt z)(j+\sqrt z)=0$ gives $j=\pm\sqrt z$, which commutes with $i$, so $j\in A_+\cap A_-=0$, a contradiction. So $z<0$, and $j/\sqrt{-z}$ squares to $-1$.

steps.slogan: Read off the quaternion multiplication table from $1,i,j,ij$.
steps.detail: Now $A=\mathbb{C}\oplus j\mathbb{C}$ has the basis $1,i,j,k=ij$ with $i^2=j^2=-1$ and $ji=-ij$, so $k^2=-1$. These are the relations of the [quaternions](c:quaternion), so $A\cong\mathbb{H}$. If $A_-=0$, then $A=A_+=\mathbb{C}$.

concepts.c:associative-algebra: Associativity makes conjugation by $i$ an algebra automorphism.
concepts.c:division-algebra: Invertibility makes multiplication by $j$ injective and removes zero divisors.
concepts.c:quaternion: The quaternion relations are the end point of the argument.
concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: Finite dimension bounds the pieces and gives algebraic elements.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: The minimal polynomial of $x$ has degree $2$ and gives a copy of $\mathbb{C}$.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closure of $\mathbb{C}$ forces the commutant to equal $\mathbb{C}$.

source.note: The classical argument through the commutant of a copy of the complex numbers; own write-up.

statement: Let $(M,\omega)$ be a compact [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold), $J$ an [almost complex structure](c:almost-complex-structure) tamed by $\omega$, and $(\Sigma,j)$ a closed Riemann surface. Let $u_\nu\colon\Sigma\to M$ be [pseudoholomorphic curves](c:pseudoholomorphic-curve) with $\int u_\nu^*\omega\le E$. Then a subsequence converges in the Gromov sense to a $J$-holomorphic map with finitely many trees of $J$-holomorphic spheres (bubbles) attached at nodes.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $(M,\omega)$ is a compact [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) and $J$ is an almost complex structure tamed by $\omega$.
Each $u_\nu\colon(\Sigma,j)\to(M,J)$ is a [pseudoholomorphic curve](c:pseudoholomorphic-curve) from one fixed closed Riemann surface.
The energy $\int_\Sigma u_\nu^*\omega$ is at most $E$ for every $\nu$.

conclusion: A subsequence of $(u_\nu)$ converges in the Gromov sense to a nodal $J$-holomorphic curve: a limit map plus finitely many bubble trees.

proofs.name: Bubbling and rescaling
proofs.slogan: Small energy gives gradient bounds, energy concentrates at finitely many points, and rescaling there produces bubble trees.
proofs.scope: An outline of Gromov's proof in the original setting: fixed domain, fixed $J$, energy bound. The versions with varying $J_\nu\to J$ and varying domains need Deligne-Mumford compactness and are not covered; the analysis of necks rests on the cited work.

roles.why: Compactness and tameness give uniform bounds on $J$ and make the energy control $|du|^2$.
The holomorphic equation gives elliptic regularity and the mean value inequality.
The energy bound limits the number of concentration points and bubbles.

steps.slogan: Bound the gradient where the energy is small.
steps.detail: A mean value inequality for $J$-holomorphic maps gives $\sup|du|\le C/r$ on a disc of radius $r/2$ whenever the energy on the disc of radius $r$ is below a constant $\varepsilon_0$. Elliptic bootstrapping then bounds all derivatives.

steps.slogan: Locate the finitely many points where energy concentrates.
steps.detail: At most $E/\varepsilon_0$ points can carry energy at least $\varepsilon_0$ in the limit. Away from them the $u_\nu$ have bounded derivatives, so a subsequence converges in $C^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}$ to a $J$-holomorphic map $u$.

steps.slogan: Rescale at a concentration point to extract a bubble.
steps.detail:
Rescale $u_
u$ near the point by the blow-up factor $|du_
u(x_
u)|	o\infty$. The rescaled maps have bounded gradient and converge to a nonconstant $J$-holomorphic map of the plane with finite energy. Gromov's removable singularity theorem extends it to a $J$-holomorphic sphere of energy at least $\varepsilon_0$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the rescaling to build a finite tree of bubbles.
steps.detail: Each bubble takes at least $\varepsilon_0$ of the total energy $E$. So after finitely many rescalings at the remaining concentration points, no further bubbles form, and the bubbles attach in trees.

steps.slogan: Show that the neck regions lose no energy and no distance.
steps.detail: In a neck between a bubble and its parent, the maps have small energy on long cylinders. Exponential decay of the energy then shows that the necks have small image diameter and carry no energy in the limit, so the images are connected at the nodes.

steps.slogan: Assemble the limit map and the bubble trees into a nodal curve.
steps.detail: The limit $u$ and the bubble trees, glued at the nodes, form a $J$-holomorphic nodal curve. The energies add up to $\lim\int u_\nu^*\omega$, and $u_\nu$ converges to it in the Gromov sense.

concepts.c:symplectic-manifold: The symplectic form defines the energy and its uniform control.
concepts.c:almost-complex-structure: The structure $J$ gives the holomorphic equation and the elliptic estimates.
concepts.c:pseudoholomorphic-curve: The curves are the objects that converge and bubble.

source.ref: M. Gromov, Pseudo holomorphic curves in symplectic manifolds, Inventiones Mathematicae 82 (1985), 307-347
source.note: Gromov's original proof; C. Hummel, Gromov's Compactness Theorem for Pseudo-holomorphic Curves (Birkhauser, 1997), gives a detailed account.

statement: Take two countries, two goods $X,Y$ and two factors $K,L$. Let both countries share the same constant-returns [production functions](c:production-function) and the same homothetic [preferences](c:preference-relation), with $X$ more capital-intensive than $Y$ at every factor price ratio. In a free-trade [equilibrium](c:competitive-equilibrium) with both goods produced everywhere, if $K/L>K^*/L^*$ at Home, then Home exports $X$ and Foreign exports $Y$.

hypotheses.text: Both countries use the same constant-returns [production functions](c:production-function), and $X$ is more capital-intensive than $Y$ at every factor price ratio.
Both countries have the same homothetic [preferences](c:preference-relation).
The countries are in a free-trade [competitive equilibrium](c:competitive-equilibrium): equal goods prices, zero profits, balanced trade and a cleared world market.
Both countries produce both goods and fully employ their capital and labour.
Home is capital-abundant: $K/L>K^*/L^*$.

conclusion: Home exports the capital-intensive good $X$, and Foreign exports the labour-intensive good $Y$.

proofs.name: Factor price equalization and homothetic demand
proofs.slogan: Equal goods prices equalize factor prices, so the capital-abundant country makes relatively more $X$ and exports it.
proofs.scope: Both claims of the theorem, under incomplete specialization, so that factor prices equalize. Models with specialization, many goods or many factors are other members of the family.

roles.why: Common technology with a fixed factor-intensity ordering ties factor prices to goods prices.
Common goods prices and zero profits fix the factor prices, and balanced trade with a cleared market fixes the sign of trade.
Zero profits hold in both industries, and full employment gives the factor-use equations.
Homothetic demand at common prices gives the same consumption ratio in both countries.
A higher capital-labour ratio at Home gives Home a larger labour share in $X$.

steps.slogan: Show that equal goods prices give equal factor prices and input coefficients.
steps.detail: Zero profit gives $p_i=c_i(w,r)$ in each country. By Shephard's lemma, $d\ln(c_X/c_Y)/d\ln w=\theta_{LX}-\theta_{LY}<0$ at every $w/r$, because $X$ is capital-intensive, so $p_X/p_Y$ fixes $w/r$. Both countries then share $w/r$, the coefficients $a_{ij}$ and $k_X>k_Y$.

steps.slogan: Write the endowment ratio as a weighted average of the two factor intensities.
steps.detail: Let $\lambda=a_{LX}Q_X/L$ be the labour share in $X$. Full employment gives $K/L=\lambda k_X+(1-\lambda)k_Y$, which increases with $\lambda$ because $k_X>k_Y$. So $K/L>K^*/L^*$ gives $\lambda>\lambda^*$.

steps.slogan: Show that Home produces relatively more $X$ than Foreign.
steps.detail: With common coefficients, $Q_X=\lambda L/a_{LX}$ and $Q_Y=(1-\lambda)L/a_{LY}$, so $Q_X/Q_Y=\dfrac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}\cdot\dfrac{a_{LY}}{a_{LX}}$. This ratio increases with $\lambda$. Hence Home has $Q_X/Q_Y>Q_X^*/Q_Y^*$.

steps.slogan: Show that both countries consume $X$ and $Y$ in the same ratio $c$.
steps.detail: Identical homothetic preferences make the demand ratio depend on the price ratio only. Both countries face the same prices, so $C_X/C_Y=C_X^*/C_Y^*=c$.

steps.slogan: Compare production and consumption ratios and use market clearing to sign the trade.
steps.detail: Balanced trade gives $p_XE_X+p_YE_Y=0$ for the net exports $E_i=Q_i-C_i$, so $E_X>0$ exactly when $Q_X/Q_Y>c$ and $E_X<0$ exactly when $Q_X/Q_Y<c$. Market clearing gives $E_X+E_X^*=0$. If $E_X\le 0$, then $Q_X^*/Q_Y^*\ge c\ge Q_X/Q_Y$, which contradicts step 3. So $E_X>0$ and $E_X^*<0$, and $E_Y<0<E_Y^*$.

concepts.c:production-function: Constant returns give unit input coefficients that depend on factor prices only.
concepts.c:preference-relation: Homothetic preferences make the consumption ratio depend on prices only.
concepts.c:competitive-equilibrium: Equilibrium supplies zero profits, equal prices, balanced trade and market clearing.

source.note: The textbook two-by-two argument by factor price equalization, homothetic demand and balanced trade; assumes incomplete specialization.

statement: Let $L$ be a finite [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) and $f,g\colon L\to[0,\infty)$ with $\sum f=\sum g$ and $f(a)g(b)\le f(a\wedge b)\,g(a\vee b)$ for all $a,b$. Then $\sum_a\varphi(a)f(a)\le\sum_a\varphi(a)g(a)$ for every monotone $\varphi\colon L\to[0,\infty)$. For probability weights, $g$ [stochastically dominates](c:stochastic-domination) $f$.

hypotheses.text: The set $L$ is a finite [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice).
The weights $f,g\colon L\to[0,\infty)$ have equal total mass $\sum_a f(a)=\sum_a g(a)$.
The inequality $f(a)g(b)\le f(a\wedge b)\,g(a\vee b)$ holds for all $a,b\in L$.
The test function $\varphi\colon L\to[0,\infty)$ is [monotone](c:monotone-function).

formal.difference: mathlib proves it for functions into a linearly ordered commutative semiring, with $\varphi$ nonnegative and monotone; the real case is an instance. The form for signed monotone $\varphi$ follows by adding a constant, since the total masses agree.

proofs.name: Four functions inequality
proofs.slogan: Feed the four functions $g$, $\varphi f$, $f$, $\varphi g$ to the Ahlswede-Daykin inequality and divide by the common mass.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, with both index sets equal to $L$ in the four functions inequality. If $f=0$ or $g=0$, the equal sums force both to vanish and the claim reads $0\le 0$.

roles.why: The four functions inequality holds on finite distributive lattices, and the meet and join appear in it.
Nonnegativity makes the four functions nonnegative, and equal masses cancel at the end.
The Holley condition gives half of the pointwise hypothesis of the four functions inequality.
Monotonicity of $\varphi$ gives the other half, $\varphi(b)\le\varphi(a\vee b)$.

steps.slogan: Dispose of the case where $f$ or $g$ is zero.
steps.detail: If $f=0$, then $\sum g=\sum f=0$ and $g\ge 0$ give $g=0$, so both sides are $0$. The case $g=0$ is symmetric. From now on $\sum f=\sum g>0$.

steps.slogan: Choose the four functions $g$, $\varphi f$, $f$, $\varphi g$ and both index sets equal to $L$.
steps.detail: All four are nonnegative because $f$, $g$ and $\varphi$ are. The four functions inequality then compares $\sum g\cdot\sum\varphi f$ with $\sum f\cdot\sum\varphi g$, which is the claim up to the common mass.

steps.slogan: Check that $g(a)\varphi(b)f(b)\le f(a\wedge b)\varphi(a\vee b)g(a\vee b)$ for all $a,b$.
steps.detail: The Holley condition with $a$ and $b$ swapped gives $f(b)g(a)\le f(a\wedge b)\,g(a\vee b)$. Monotonicity gives $\varphi(b)\le\varphi(a\vee b)$. Multiply the two nonnegative inequalities.

steps.slogan: Apply the Ahlswede-Daykin inequality to the four functions.
steps.detail: It gives $\sum g\cdot\sum\varphi f\le\sum f\cdot\sum\varphi g$, because both index sets are $L$ and so $L\wedge L=L\vee L=L$.

steps.slogan: Divide by the common positive mass to obtain the claim.
steps.detail: With $\sum f=\sum g=m>0$, the inequality reads $m\sum\varphi f\le m\sum\varphi g$. Division by $m$ gives $\sum\varphi f\le\sum\varphi g$.

concepts.c:distributive-lattice: Distributivity is the setting of the four functions inequality.
concepts.c:stochastic-domination: The inequality for all monotone $\varphi$ is stochastic domination.

source.note: mathlib splits off f = 0 and g = 0, then applies four_functions_theorem to g, mu * f, f, mu * g with univ for both sets.

statement: Let $u_1,u_2$ be [distributions](c:distribution) on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $X$ whose [wave front sets](c:wave-front-set) satisfy: no $(x,\xi)\in\mathrm{WF}(u_1)$ has $(x,-\xi)\in\mathrm{WF}(u_2)$. Then $u_1u_2=\Delta^*(u_1\otimes u_2)$ is a well-defined distribution that extends the product of smooth functions, with $\mathrm{WF}(u_1u_2)\subseteq\mathrm{WF}(u_1)\cup\mathrm{WF}(u_2)\cup(\mathrm{WF}(u_1)+\mathrm{WF}(u_2))$.

hypotheses.text: The objects $u_1,u_2$ are [distributions](c:distribution) on a smooth manifold $X$.
No covector $\xi$ at a point $x$ lies in $\mathrm{WF}(u_1)$ while $-\xi$ lies in $\mathrm{WF}(u_2)$.

conclusion: The product $u_1u_2$ exists as a distribution, equals the usual product for smooth factors and obeys the stated wave front bound.

proofs.name: Pullback by the diagonal
proofs.slogan: Form the tensor product on $X\times X$, check that its wave front set misses the conormal of the diagonal, and pull it back.
proofs.scope: An outline of Hormander's proof, which rests on his theorems on tensor products and pullbacks of distributions. Products under other conditions, such as a Sobolev regularity condition, are other members of the family.

roles.why: The tensor product $u_1\otimes u_2$ and the pullback act on distributions.
The condition makes the wave front set of the tensor product miss the conormal of the diagonal.

steps.slogan: Form the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $u_1\otimes u_2$ and bound its wave front set.
steps.detail: The distribution $u_1\otimes u_2$ on $X\times X$ has $\mathrm{WF}(u_1\otimes u_2)\subseteq(\mathrm{WF}(u_1)\times\mathrm{WF}(u_2))\cup(\mathrm{WF}(u_1)\times 0)\cup(0\times\mathrm{WF}(u_2))$ (Hormander, theorem 8.2.9).

steps.slogan: Identify the [conormal bundle](c:conormal-bundle) of the diagonal $\Delta\colon X\to X\times X$.
steps.detail: Covectors that vanish on the tangent space of the diagonal are those of the form $(x,x;\xi,-\xi)$. These form the conormal set $N_\Delta$ of $\Delta$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\mathrm{WF}(u_1\otimes u_2)$ misses the conormal set $N_\Delta$.
steps.detail: A point of the first piece in $N_\Delta$ would give $\xi\in\mathrm{WF}(u_1)$ and $-\xi\in\mathrm{WF}(u_2)$, which the hypothesis excludes. A point of the other two pieces has the form $(\xi,0)$ or $(0,\eta)$, which lies in $N_\Delta$ only for the zero covector, and the wave front set has none.

steps.slogan: Apply the pullback theorem for smooth maps whose conormal set misses the wave front set.
steps.detail: For a smooth map $\Delta$ and a closed cone $\Gamma$ with $\Gamma\cap N_\Delta=\varnothing$, pullback extends uniquely from smooth functions to distributions with wave front set in $\Gamma$, continuously, with $\mathrm{WF}(\Delta^*v)\subseteq\Delta^*\mathrm{WF}(v)$ (Hormander, theorem 8.2.4).

steps.slogan: Define $u_1u_2=\Delta^*(u_1\otimes u_2)$ and read off its properties.
steps.detail: By steps 3 and 4 this [pullback](c:pullback) exists. It equals the usual product for smooth factors, since pullback extends the smooth case. Computing $\Delta^*\mathrm{WF}(u_1\otimes u_2)$ gives $\mathrm{WF}(u_1u_2)\subseteq\mathrm{WF}(u_1)\cup\mathrm{WF}(u_2)\cup(\mathrm{WF}(u_1)+\mathrm{WF}(u_2))$.

concepts.c:distribution: The factors and the product are distributions.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The diagonal embeds the manifold $X$ in $X\times X$.
concepts.c:wave-front-set: The wave front sets decide whether the pullback to the diagonal exists.
concepts.c:tensor-product: The tensor product carries the two factors to $X\times X$.
concepts.c:conormal-bundle: The conormal set of the diagonal is what the wave front set must avoid.
concepts.c:pullback: The product is the pullback of the tensor product along the diagonal.

source.ref: L. Hormander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis, 2nd edition, Springer, 1990, theorems 8.2.4, 8.2.9 and 8.2.10
source.note: Theorem 8.2.10 is this criterion; its proof combines the tensor product theorem 8.2.9 with the pullback theorem 8.2.4.

statement: Let $A$ be a $*$-subalgebra of the bounded operators $B(H)$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$, and let $M$ be its closure in the [strong operator topology](c:strong-operator-topology). Then the [unit ball](c:unit-ball) of $A$ is strongly dense in the unit ball of $M$, and the self-adjoint part of the ball of $A$ is strongly dense in that of $M$.

hypotheses.text: The set $A\subseteq B(H)$ is a subalgebra that is closed under adjoints.
The set $M$ is the closure of $A$ in the [strong operator topology](c:strong-operator-topology).

conclusion: Every operator of norm at most $1$ in $M$ is a strong limit of a net of operators of norm at most $1$ in $A$, self-adjoint if the operator is.

proofs.name: Bounded function and matrix trick
proofs.slogan: Approximate a self-adjoint element through the bounded function $2t/(1+t^2)$, then reach all elements by $2\times2$ matrices.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for any $*$-subalgebra; when $A$ acts nondegenerately, $M$ is a [von Neumann algebra](c:von-neumann-algebra). Strong closure here means closure of the set, with nets.

roles.why: Closure under adjoints and products makes $A_{sa}$ convex and lets functions of its elements stay in $A$.
Strong limits of elements of $A$ are the elements of $M$ that we must approximate.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a norm-closed algebra.
steps.detail: Let $\bar A$ be the norm closure of $A$, a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) with the same strong closure $M$. If $x\in\bar A$ and $\|x\|\le 1$, pick $a\in A$ with $\|x-a\|<\varepsilon$; then $a/(1+\varepsilon)$ lies in the ball of $A$ and is within $2\varepsilon$ of $x$. So the ball of $A$ is norm dense in that of $\bar A$, and we may assume $A=\bar A$.

steps.slogan: Show that the self-adjoint part of $A$ is strongly dense in that of $M$.
steps.detail: If $h\in M$ is self-adjoint, a net $a_\lambda\in A$ converges strongly, hence weakly, to $h$. Then $(a_\lambda+a_\lambda^*)/2\to h$ weakly, because the adjoint is weakly continuous. The convex set $A_{sa}$ has the same weak and strong closures, so $h$ is a strong limit of elements of $A_{sa}$, with no control of their norms.

steps.slogan: Tame the norms with the bounded function $f(t)=2t/(1+t^2)$.
steps.detail: The function $f$ is real, vanishes at infinity, has $|f|\le 1$, and maps $[-1,1]$ onto itself with inverse $g(s)=(1-\sqrt{1-s^2})/s$. By the resolvent identity for $(1+it)^{-1}$ and the Stone-Weierstrass theorem, $a\mapsto f(a)$ is strongly continuous on self-adjoint operators.

steps.slogan: Approximate a self-adjoint $h$ of norm at most $1$ by $f(a_\lambda)$.
steps.detail: Put $k=g(h)\in M$ by [continuous functional calculus](c:continuous-functional-calculus), so $f(k)=h$. Take self-adjoint $a_\lambda\in A$ with $a_\lambda\to k$ strongly. Then $f(a_\lambda)\to h$ strongly, $f(a_\lambda)\in A$, and $\|f(a_\lambda)\|\le 1$.

steps.slogan: Reach a general operator through a self-adjoint $2\times2$ operator matrix.
steps.detail: Apply steps 2 to 4 to $M_2(A)$ on $H\oplus H$, whose strong closure is $M_2(M)$. For $x\in M$ with $\|x\|\le1$, the self-adjoint $y=\begin{pmatrix}0&x\\x^*&0\end{pmatrix}$ has $\|y\|\le 1$, so $y=\lim y_\lambda$ strongly with $y_\lambda$ self-adjoint of norm at most $1$ in $M_2(A)$. The upper right entries $b_\lambda\in A$ have norm at most $1$ and converge strongly to $x$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The algebra acts on a Hilbert space, and strong convergence is pointwise on vectors.
concepts.c:strong-operator-topology: The theorem asks for density in this topology.
concepts.c:unit-ball: The balls are the sets in which density is proved.
concepts.c:von-neumann-algebra: The strong closure of a nondegenerate $*$-algebra is a von Neumann algebra.
concepts.c:c-star-algebra: The norm closure is a C*-algebra, which is closed under functional calculus.
concepts.c:continuous-functional-calculus: It gives $g(h)$ and $f(a_\lambda)$ as elements of the algebras.

source.note: The classical proof by the function 2t/(1+t^2) and the 2x2 matrix trick, as in Murphy, C*-algebras and Operator Theory, section 4.3, and in Kadison and Ringrose.

statement: Let $F_1,\dots,F_k$ be [intersecting families](c:intersecting-family) of subsets of an $n$-element set, with $n\ge 1$. Then $|F_1\cup\dots\cup F_k|\le 2^n-2^{\max(n-k,0)}$. For $k\le n$ the bound is $2^n-2^{n-k}$.

hypotheses.text: The ground set has $n\ge 1$ elements.
Each $F_i$ is an [intersecting family](c:intersecting-family): any two of its sets share an element.

conclusion: The union $F_1\cup\dots\cup F_k$ has at most $2^n-2^{\max(n-k,0)}$ members.

proofs.name: Maximal families and Harris-Kleitman
proofs.slogan: Extend each family to a maximal intersecting upper set, then bound the overlap of the union by the Harris-Kleitman inequality, by induction on $k$.
proofs.scope: All $k$. The case $k\ge n$ is direct; for $k\le n$ the induction starts at $k=0$, where the union is empty.

roles.why: The ground set has $2^n$ subsets, which sets the size of every extended family and the complements.
No intersecting family holds the empty set, and each one extends to a maximal intersecting family.

steps.slogan: Settle the case $k\ge n$ by excluding the empty set.
steps.detail: An intersecting family never contains $\varnothing$, because $\varnothing\cap\varnothing=\varnothing$. So the union lies in the $2^n-1$ nonempty subsets, which is the bound $2^n-2^0$ for $k\ge n$.

steps.slogan: Extend each family to a maximal intersecting family, an upper set of size $2^{n-1}$.
steps.detail: Let $F_i'\supseteq F_i$ be maximal intersecting. If $A\in F_i'$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $F_i'\cup\{B\}$ is intersecting, so $B\in F_i'$ and $F_i'$ is an [upper set](c:upper-set). If neither $A$ nor its complement lay in $F_i'$, maximality gives $B,C\in F_i'$ with $B\subseteq A^c$ and $C\subseteq A$ and $B\cap C=\varnothing$, which is impossible; so $|F_i'|=2^{n-1}$.

steps.slogan: Split the union into the first family and the part of the rest outside it.
steps.detail: For $k\le n$ let $U=F_2'\cup\dots\cup F_k'$, an upper set. Then $|F_1\cup\dots\cup F_k|\le|F_1'|+|U\setminus F_1'|=2^{n-1}+|U\cap(F_1')^c|$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|U\cap(F_1')^c|$ by the Harris-Kleitman inequality for an upper set and a lower set.
steps.detail: The complement of the upper set $F_1'$ is a lower set with $2^{n-1}$ members. The inequality gives $|U\cap(F_1')^c|\le|U|\cdot 2^{n-1}/2^n=|U|/2$.

steps.slogan: Insert the induction bound for $U$ and simplify to $2^n-2^{n-k}$.
steps.detail: The families $F_2',\dots,F_k'$ are intersecting, so induction gives $|U|\le 2^n-2^{n-k+1}$. Hence $|F_1\cup\dots\cup F_k|\le 2^{n-1}+\tfrac12(2^n-2^{n-k+1})=2^n-2^{n-k}$.

steps.slogan: Combine both cases into the bound $2^n-2^{\max(n-k,0)}$.
steps.detail: For $k\ge n$, step 1 gives $2^n-1$. For $k\le n$, steps 2 to 5 give $2^n-2^{n-k}$ by induction on $k$. The two cases cover every $k$.

concepts.c:intersecting-family: The hypothesis excludes the empty set and allows extension to a maximal family.
concepts.c:upper-set: Upper sets are the sets to which the Harris-Kleitman inequality applies.

source.note: mathlib inducts on the number of families: it extends each to a maximal intersecting family (Set.Intersecting.exists_card_eq, an upper set) and bounds the overlap with IsUpperSet.card_inter_le_finset (Harris-Kleitman).

statement: Let $f$ be a [univalent function](c:univalent-function) on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, that is, [analytic](c:analytic-function) and injective. Then $f(\mathbb{D})$ contains the disk with center $f(0)$ and radius $|f'(0)|/4$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) on $\mathbb{D}$.
The function $f$ is injective on $\mathbb{D}$.

proofs.name: Area theorem and a coefficient bound
proofs.slogan: Bound the second coefficient by $2$ with the area theorem, then apply the bound to a Mobius transform that omits a value.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, after normalizing to $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$. The coefficient bound $|a_2|\le 2$ is proved on the way; the sharp bounds for all coefficients (de Branges) are not used.

roles.why: Analyticity gives the power series $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots$ and the analytic square root.
Injectivity makes $\psi$ univalent for the area theorem and keeps the Mobius transform of $f$ injective.

steps.slogan: Normalize $f$ so that $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$.
steps.detail: An injective analytic function has $f'(0)\ne 0$. Replace $f$ by $(f-f(0))/f'(0)$, which is again univalent. The claim becomes $\{|w|<1/4\}\subseteq f(\mathbb{D})$ for $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots$.

steps.slogan: Take the odd square root of $f(z^2)$ and invert it to a function $\psi$ on $|\zeta|>1$.
steps.detail: As $f(z^2)/z^2$ has no zeros on the simply connected $\mathbb{D}$, it has an analytic square root equal to $1$ at $0$, so $\varphi(z)=\sqrt{f(z^2)}=z+\tfrac{a_2}{2}z^3+\cdots$ is odd and injective. Then $\psi(\zeta)=1/\varphi(1/\zeta)=\zeta-\tfrac{a_2}{2}\zeta^{-1}+\cdots$ is univalent on $|\zeta|>1$.

steps.slogan: Apply the area theorem to $\psi$ to get $|a_2|\le 2$.
steps.detail: The area theorem says that $\sum_{n\ge1}n|b_n|^2\le 1$ for a univalent $\zeta+b_0+\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\zeta^{-n}$. Here $b_1=-a_2/2$, so $|a_2|^2/4\le 1$.

steps.slogan: Omit a value $w$ and form the Mobius transform $h=wf/(w-f)$.
steps.detail: Suppose $w\notin f(\mathbb{D})$. Then $h=wf/(w-f)$ is analytic and injective, because $t\mapsto wt/(w-t)$ is injective off $w$. Also $h(z)=z+(a_2+1/w)z^2+\cdots$.

steps.slogan: Apply the coefficient bound to $f$ and to $h$ to get $|w|\ge 1/4$.
steps.detail: Step 3 applies to every normalized univalent function, so $|a_2|\le 2$ and $|a_2+1/w|\le 2$. Then $1/|w|\le|a_2+1/w|+|a_2|\le 4$. Every omitted value has $|w|\ge 1/4$, so $\{|w|<1/4\}\subseteq f(\mathbb{D})$.

concepts.c:univalent-function: Univalence makes the area theorem and the Mobius transform apply.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Analytic functions have the power series whose second coefficient is bounded.

source.note: The classical proof by the area theorem and the bound |a_2| <= 2, as in Duren, Univalent Functions (Springer, 1983).

statement: Let $E$ be a Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ and let $s\subseteq E$ be a nonempty [compact](c:compact-space) set. Then $s$ has an [extreme point](c:extreme-point).

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) over $\mathbb{R}$.
The set $s\subseteq E$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
The set $s$ is nonempty.

conclusion: Some point of $s$ is an extreme point of $s$.

proofs.name: Minimal closed extreme subset
proofs.slogan: Take a minimal nonempty closed extreme subset by Zorn's lemma, and show by Hahn-Banach that it is one point.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The set $s$ is nonempty, so the family of its nonempty closed extreme subsets is nonempty.

roles.why: Hausdorff makes compact sets closed, and local convexity gives a separating functional.
Compactness gives nonempty intersections of chains and a maximizer of the functional.
A nonempty $s$ is a member of the family, so Zorn's lemma has a start.

steps.slogan: Collect the nonempty closed [extreme subsets](c:is-extreme) of $s$ into a family $\mathcal S$.
steps.detail: A subset $t\subseteq s$ is extreme in $s$ if an open segment with ends in $s$ that meets $t$ lies in $t$. The set $s$ is closed, because it is compact in a Hausdorff space, so $s\in\mathcal S$.

steps.slogan: Show that every chain in $\mathcal S$ has a lower bound, and take a minimal member $t$.
steps.detail: The intersection of a chain is closed and extreme. It is nonempty, because the chain consists of nonempty closed subsets of the compact $s$ and has the finite intersection property. Zorn's lemma, for the reverse inclusion, gives a minimal $t\in\mathcal S$.

steps.slogan: Suppose $t$ has two points $x\ne y$ and separate them by a continuous linear functional.
steps.detail: Because $E$ is Hausdorff and locally convex, the Hahn-Banach separation theorem gives a continuous linear $\ell\colon E\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\ell(x)<\ell(y)$.

steps.slogan: Take the maximizers of $\ell$ on $t$ to get a smaller member of $\mathcal S$.
steps.detail: The continuous $\ell$ attains its maximum on the compact $t$, so $t'=\{z\in t:\ell(z)=\max_t\ell\}$ is nonempty and closed. It is extreme in $t$ because $\ell$ is linear, hence extreme in $s$. Since $x\notin t'$, we get $t'\subsetneq t$, which contradicts minimality.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $t=\{x\}$ and that $x$ is an extreme point of $s$.
steps.detail: So $t$ has exactly one point $x$, as $t\ne\varnothing$. The set $\{x\}$ is extreme in $s$, which says that $x$ is an extreme point of $s$.

concepts.c:locally-convex-space: Local convexity and Hausdorff give the separating functional.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives nonempty chain intersections and maximizers.
concepts.c:extreme-point: The extreme point is the conclusion of the argument.
concepts.c:is-extreme: Minimal extreme subsets are the objects of the Zorn argument.

source.note: mathlib applies zorn_superset to the nonempty closed extreme subsets, uses IsCompact.nonempty_iInter_of_directed_nonempty_isCompact_isClosed for chains, and geometric_hahn_banach_point_point with IsCompact.exists_isMaxOn for a minimal set.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring), $I$ an ideal generated by $n$ elements, and $\mathfrak p$ a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) minimal over $I$. Then the [height](c:height) of $\mathfrak p$ is at most $n$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a commutative [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring).
The ideal $I$ is generated by $n$ elements $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
The ideal $\mathfrak p$ is a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) that is minimal among the primes containing $I$.

conclusion: The height of $\mathfrak p$ is at most $n$.

formal.difference: mathlib bounds the height by the minimal number of generators of $I$, a cardinal read in the extended naturals. For an $n$-generated ideal that number is at most $n$, so the statements agree.

proofs.name: Induction on the number of generators
proofs.slogan: Localize, pass to a prime covered by $\mathfrak p$, and use the principal ideal theorem to cut one generator by induction.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for every $n\ge0$. For $n=0$ the ideal is $0$ and the minimal prime has height $0$.

roles.why: Noetherianity gives the principal ideal theorem, finite generation of $\mathfrak p$ and minimal primes inside a given prime.
The $n$ generators supply $x_1$ and the $n-1$ elements $y_i$ for the induction.
Minimality over $I$ makes $\mathfrak p$ the only prime above $\mathfrak q+(x_1)$ and survives localization and quotients.

steps.slogan: Localize at $\mathfrak p$ to make the ring local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p$.
steps.detail: The [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is Noetherian, $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$ is minimal over $IR_{\mathfrak p}$, and the height is unchanged. So assume that $R$ is a [local ring](c:local-ring) with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p$.

steps.slogan: Induct on $n$ and reduce to a prime $\mathfrak q$ covered by $\mathfrak p$.
steps.detail: For $n=0$, $I=0$ and a minimal prime has height $0$. For $n\ge1$ it suffices to show $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\le n-1$ for every prime $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ with no prime strictly between, because every chain of primes below $\mathfrak p$ extends to one that ends in such a $\mathfrak q$ ($\mathfrak p$ is finitely generated, so Zorn applies).

steps.slogan: Choose a generator $x_1\notin\mathfrak q$ and write the other generators modulo $x_1$.
steps.detail: Some $x_i\notin\mathfrak q$, since $I\subseteq\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ contradicts minimality; call it $x_1$. The only prime above $\mathfrak q+(x_1)$ is $\mathfrak p$, so $\mathfrak p$ is the [radical](c:radical) of $\mathfrak q+(x_1)$ and $x_i^N=y_i+a_ix_1$ with $y_i\in\mathfrak q$ for $i=2,\dots,n$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathfrak q$ is minimal over $J=(y_2,\dots,y_n)$.
steps.detail: Take a prime $\mathfrak q'\subseteq\mathfrak q$ minimal over $J$. In the domain $R/\mathfrak q'$, the image of $\mathfrak p$ is minimal over $(\bar x_1)$, because a power of every $\bar x_i$ lies in $(\bar x_1)$. The principal ideal theorem gives height at most $1$ there, so $\bar{\mathfrak q}\subsetneq\bar{\mathfrak p}$ has height $0$, $\bar{\mathfrak q}=0$ and $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak q'$.

steps.slogan: Apply the induction hypothesis to $\mathfrak q$ and $J$.
steps.detail: The ideal $J$ has $n-1$ generators and $\mathfrak q$ is minimal over it, so $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\le n-1$. By step 2, $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\le n$.

concepts.c:noetherian-ring: Noetherianity gives the principal ideal theorem and finite generation of primes.
concepts.c:prime-ideal: The theorem bounds the length of chains of prime ideals.
concepts.c:height: The height is the quantity bounded, through covered primes.
concepts.c:local-ring: In a local ring $\mathfrak p$ is the only maximal ideal.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: Localizing at $\mathfrak p$ keeps the height and makes the ring local.
concepts.c:radical: The radical of $\mathfrak q+(x_1)$ is $\mathfrak p$, which gives the powers $x_i^N$.

source.note: mathlib localizes at p, inducts strongly on the number of generators through covering primes (height_le_iff_covBy), and shows q minimal over the smaller ideal in mem_minimalPrimes_span_of_mem_minimalPrimes_span_insert with the principal ideal theorem.

statement: Let the seven bridges of Konigsberg join four land masses $A,B,C,D$ as a [graph](c:graph) with two bridges each for $AB$ and $AC$ and one each for $AD$, $BD$, $CD$. Then no walk crosses every bridge exactly once.

hypotheses.text: The bridges form a [graph](c:graph) on the land masses $A,B,C,D$ with two bridges each for $AB$ and $AC$ and one each for $AD$, $BD$, $CD$.

conclusion: No walk along the bridges uses each of the seven bridges exactly once.

proofs.name: Parity of degrees
proofs.slogan: A walk that uses every bridge once leaves at most two land masses of odd degree, but Konigsberg has four.
proofs.scope: The seven-bridge layout. The argument shows more generally that such a walk needs at most two vertices of odd degree, which is one direction of Euler's theorem.

roles.why: The layout gives the degrees $5,3,3,3$ of the four land masses.

steps.slogan: Compute the [degree](c:vertex-degree) of each land mass.
steps.detail: The degrees are $\deg A=2+2+1=5$ and $\deg B=\deg C=\deg D=3$. They add to $14=2\cdot 7$, as the degree-sum formula requires.

steps.slogan: Assume that a walk crosses each bridge exactly once.
steps.detail: Write the walk as land masses $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_7$, with the seven bridges between consecutive ones, each used once.

steps.slogan: Pair the bridge of entry and the bridge of exit at each inner visit.
steps.detail: At a visit to $v_k$ with $0<k<7$, the walk enters by one bridge and leaves by another. Each bridge is used once, so the visits to a land mass use its bridges in pairs, apart from the first bridge at $v_0$ and the last at $v_7$.

steps.slogan: Show that every land mass other than $v_0$ and $v_7$ has even degree.
steps.detail: Every bridge at such a land mass is crossed once and lies in exactly one pair, so its degree is twice its number of visits. If $v_0=v_7$, every land mass has even degree. So at most two land masses have odd degree.

steps.slogan: Count four land masses of odd degree and contradict the parity result.
steps.detail: The land masses $A,B,C,D$ all have odd degree, but step 4 allows at most two. So no such walk exists.

concepts.c:graph: The land masses and bridges form a graph, and a walk is a path in it.
concepts.c:vertex-degree: The degree counts the bridges at a land mass, and its parity decides the case.

source.note: Euler's argument of 1736; only the necessity half of Euler's theorem on walks that use every edge once is used.

statement: Every natural number $n$ is a sum of four squares of [integers](c:integer): $n=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$.
conclusion: For every natural number $n$ there are integers $a,b,c,d$ with $n=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$.

proofs.name: Euler's identity and descent on primes
proofs.slogan: Reduce to primes by Euler's four-square identity, then show for a prime that the least multiple of $p$ that is a sum of four squares is $p$ itself.
proofs.scope: All natural numbers, with $0=0^2+0^2+0^2+0^2$ and $1=1^2+0^2+0^2+0^2$ treated directly. The prime $2$ is $1^2+1^2+0^2+0^2$, and the descent below treats the odd primes.

steps.slogan: Reduce to [prime numbers](c:prime-number) with Euler's four-square identity.
steps.detail: Euler's identity expresses $(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)(w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2)$ as a sum of four squares of explicit bilinear forms. So products of sums of four squares are sums of four squares, and primes suffice.

steps.slogan: Find $x,y$ with $x^2+y^2+1\equiv0$ modulo an odd prime $p$.
steps.detail: The $(p+1)/2$ residues of $x^2$ and the $(p+1)/2$ residues of $-1-y^2$ cannot be disjoint among $p$ residues. With $|x|,|y|<p/2$ this gives $x^2+y^2+1=kp$ and $0<k<p$.

steps.slogan: Take the least $m>0$ such that $mp$ is a sum of four squares.
steps.detail: Step 2 shows that such $m<p$ exist. Let $mp=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ with $m$ least. If $m=1$ we are done, so assume $1<m<p$.

steps.slogan: Produce a smaller multiple of $p$ when $m>1$, which contradicts minimality.
steps.detail: If $m$ is even, pair the four squares by parity to write $\tfrac m2p$ as a sum of four squares. If $m$ is odd, take residues $a',b',c',d'$ of least absolute value, so that the sum of their squares is $rm$ with $0<r<m$, and Euler's identity for $(rm)(mp)$ gives $rp$ as a sum of four squares.

steps.slogan: Combine the prime case with products to cover every natural number.
steps.detail: By steps 3 and 4 every prime is a sum of four squares. Every $n\ge2$ is a product of primes, and step 1 combines their representations. The cases $n=0,1$ are direct.

concepts.c:integer: The four squares are squares of integers.
concepts.c:prime-number: The proof proves the theorem for primes and multiplies the results.

source.note: mathlib proves the prime case Nat.Prime.sum_four_squares with a least multiple of p and Euler's identity (Nat.euler_four_squares), then multiplies by induction on the factorization (Nat.recOnMul).

statement: For every complex [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p(z)=\sum_k a_kz^k$, the [Mahler measure](c:mahler-measure) $M(p)=\exp\Big(\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|p(e^{i\theta})|\,d\theta\Big)$ satisfies $M(p)\le\Big(\sum_k|a_k|^2\Big)^{1/2}$, with $M(0)=0$.
conclusion: The Mahler measure of $p$ is at most the Euclidean norm $\big(\sum_k|a_k|^2\big)^{1/2}$ of its coefficient vector.

proofs.name: Jensen twice and Parseval
proofs.slogan: Move the exponential inside the circle average by Jensen's inequality, bound the mean of $|p|$ by the mean square, and evaluate that by Parseval's identity.
proofs.scope: Every polynomial, including $p=0$, where both sides are $0$. Below, $\operatorname{avg}$ denotes the mean $\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cdot\,d\theta$ over the circle.

steps.slogan: Dispose of $p=0$ and show that $\log|p|$ is integrable on the circle.
steps.detail: If $p=0$, then $M(p)=0$ and the bound holds. Otherwise $p$ has finitely many zeros, so $|p(e^{i\theta})|>0$ except at finitely many $\theta$, and the logarithmic singularities there are integrable.

steps.slogan: Apply Jensen's inequality for $\exp$ to move the exponential inside the average.
steps.detail: The exponential is [convex](c:convex-function), and $\log|p|$ is integrable by step 1. Jensen's inequality gives $M(p)=\exp(\operatorname{avg}\log|p|)\le\operatorname{avg}\exp(\log|p|)=\operatorname{avg}|p|$.

steps.slogan: Apply Jensen's inequality for the square to bound the mean of $|p|$.
steps.detail: The square is a convex function. Jensen's inequality gives $(\operatorname{avg}|p|)^2\le\operatorname{avg}|p|^2$, and taking square roots gives $\operatorname{avg}|p|\le(\operatorname{avg}|p|^2)^{1/2}$.

steps.slogan: Compute the mean square of $|p|$ by Parseval's identity.
steps.detail: The $a_k$ are the [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) of $\theta\mapsto p(e^{i\theta})$, and the functions $e^{ik\theta}$ are orthonormal for the weight $d\theta/2\pi$. So $\operatorname{avg}|p(e^{i\theta})|^2=\sum_k|a_k|^2$.

steps.slogan: Chain the three estimates to get the bound.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives $M(p)\le\operatorname{avg}|p|$, step 3 gives $\operatorname{avg}|p|\le(\operatorname{avg}|p|^2)^{1/2}$, and step 4 gives $\operatorname{avg}|p|^2=\sum_k|a_k|^2$. Together these give the bound.

concepts.c:polynomial: The polynomial supplies the coefficients and the finitely many zeros on the circle.
concepts.c:mahler-measure: The Mahler measure is the quantity bounded, as an exponential of an average.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of $\exp$ and of the square gives both Jensen steps.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: The polynomial coefficients are the Fourier coefficients on the circle.

source.note: mathlib uses Jensen's inequality twice (convexOn_exp.map_average_le and convexOn_pow 2) and Parseval's identity (Polynomial.sum_sq_norm_coeff_eq_circleAverage).
